'''''Ludwigia palustris''''' is a species of flowering plant in the [[Onagraceae|evening primrose family]] known by the common names '''marsh seedbox''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=LUPA|taxon=Ludwigia palustris|accessdate=22 December 2015}}</ref> '''Hampshire-purslane'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> and '''water purslane'''.  This is an [[aquatic plant|aquatic]] or semiaquatic perennial herb which grows in moist to wet to flooded areas. It is sometimes a [[noxious weed|weed]]. The species [[epithet]] ''palustris'' is Latin for "of the marsh" and indicates its common habitat.<ref>{{Cite book |date = 1997 | first1 = Archibald William | last1 = Smith |publisher= Dover Publications | url = {{Google Books URL|ahNMkgoNJ7IC|p=258}} |title = A Gardener's Handbook of Plant Names: Their Meanings and Origins |page=258 |isbn=9780486297156}}</ref>

== Description ==
''L. palustris'' forms [[Prostrate plant|prostrate]], sprawling mats in wet, disturbed areas. Its stems are semi-succulent, reddish in color, and smooth or slightly hairy. As the stems spread along the ground, roots form from the [[Nodes (botany)|nodes]]. At maturity, the stems may reach 10-40 cm long.<ref name=":0">Cooke, S.S, ed. 1997.  A Field Guide to the Common Wetland Plants of Western Washington and Northwestern Oregon.  Seattle Audubon Society and Washington Native Plant Society.  Seattle Ausubon Society, Seattle, WA, 417pp. Hitchcock, Leo C. and Arthur Cronquist. 1973. Flora of the Pacific Northwest.  University of Washington Press, Seattle, WA, and London, England, 730pp.</ref>

The leaves are [[Opposite (botany)|opposite]], smooth, oval-shaped, and reach up to 4 cm long. They have a [[Petiole (botany)|winged petiole]] and are often reddish-green in color.
[[File:Ludwigia palustris 258349719.jpg|thumb|Flowers with visible stamens]]
The greenish-white flowers are born on the leaf [[axils]] and reach 2-3 cm long.<ref name=":0" /> They lack [[petal]]s, and are composed of 4 triangular-shaped [[sepal]]s and 4 white-tipped [[stamen]]s, set above a cube-shaped, 4-angled [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]].

The fruits are small, cube-shaped [[Capsule (fruit)|capsules]], 2-3 cm long.<ref name=":0" /> They are pale green in color, with darker green stripes along the angles. The sepals are [[Persistence (botany)|persistent]], remaining present on the developed fruits.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ludwigia palustris (Common Water-purslane) - FSUS |url=https://fsus.ncbg.unc.edu/main.php?pg=show-taxon-detail.php&lsid=urn:lsid:ncbg.unc.edu:taxon:%7BCC02D80A-AC35-45C9-B774-489E5B011E04%7D |access-date=2026-05-03 |website=fsus.ncbg.unc.edu |language=en}}</ref>
[[File:Ludwigia palustris 258349727.jpg|thumb|Roots extending from the nodes of the stem, with axillary flowers visible]]

== Taxonomy ==
''Ludwigia palustris'' was given the scientific name ''Isnardia palustris'' in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]]. It was moved to the genus ''[[Ludwigia (plant)|Ludwigia]]'' by [[Stephen Elliott (botanist)|Stephen Elliott]] in 1817. Together with its genus it is classified in the family [[Onagraceae]]. Though it has not accepted [[Variety (botany)|varieties]], there are five variety names among its 21 [[Synonym (botany)|synonyms]].<ref name="POWO">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |date=2026 |id=30031106-2 |title=''Ludwigia palustris'' (L.) Elliott |access-date=13 March 2026}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''L. palustris'' is [[Circumpolar distribution|circumpolar]] species with a large native range. It occurs in North America, South America, Africa, Asia, and Europe. It occurs as a [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] or [[Invasive species|invasive]] species in Hawaii, Australia, and New Zealand.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Dítě |first=Daniel |last2=Jr |first2=Pavol Eliáš |last3=Dítě |first3=Zuzana |last4=Šimková |first4=Andrea |date=2017-03-31 |title=Recent distribution and phytosociological affiliation of Ludwigia palustris in Slovakia |url=https://pbsociety.org.pl/journals/index.php/asbp/article/view/asbp.3544 |journal=Acta Societatis Botanicorum Poloniae |language=en |volume=86 |issue=1 |doi=10.5586/asbp.3544 |issn=2083-9480|doi-access=free }}</ref> 

The species is generally restricted to low elevations, where it grows on shallow bodies of water such as reservoirs, ditches, and the banks of ponds, rivers, and streams. It requires wet, muddy or sandy soils poor in calcium but rich in [[humus]] and nutrients.<ref name=":1" />

== Conservation status ==
''L. palustris'' is designated by the [[IUCN Red List]] and [[NatureServe]] as a secure (G5) species globally. In North America, it is also designated as secure (N5) in both Canada and the United States. In some states and provinces, it is designated to be at higher risk. In both Arizona and Prince Edward Island, it is [[Subnational rank|ranked]] as a critically imperiled (S1) species. In New Mexico it is imperiled (S2). In Kansas, Iowa, and Quebec it is vulnerable (S3).<ref name="NatureServe"/>

The plant can be highly invasive outside its native range, very adaptable, and reproduces asexually.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |title=Biological control of invasive water primroses, ''Ludwigia'' spp., in the United States: A feasibility assessment |date=2021 |url=https://ucanr.edu/sites/DRAAWP/files/358397.pdf | journal = Journal of Aquatic Plant Management | series = 59 | pages = 67–77}}</ref> ''Ludwigia palustris'' poses a potential threat to wetland vegetation in Victoria, Australia. It has spread to riverbanks in Northeastern Australia and other areas.<ref name="weedsofaustralia">{{Cite web |title=Weeds of Australia - Fact Sheet ''Ludwigia Palustris'' |url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/ludwigia_palustris.htm |access-date=24 October 2024}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
''L. palustris'' is cultivated for use in aquariums and [[aquascaping]]. It is often sold under the names Ludwigia 'super red', Ludwigia 'mini super red', or Ludwigia 'red'.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Aquarist |first=The 2Hr |title=How to grow Ludwigia sp. 'Super red' |url=https://www.2hraquarist.com/blogs/freshwater-aquarium-plants-guide/how-to-grow-ludwigia-sp-red |access-date=2026-01-01 |website=The 2Hr Aquarist |language=en}}</ref>
